terms.definition: A function that turns any input into a fixed-size number, spreading inputs evenly across the range.
The remainder after division; hashing a key and taking it modulo N picks one of N slots.
One server in a group, such as one cache or one database shard.

before.note: Read Caching first: consistent hashing is how a cache or data cluster decides which node holds each key. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: When data is spread across several nodes, something has to decide which node holds each key. The obvious way is to hash the key and take it modulo the number of nodes. That works until the number of nodes changes: add or remove one, and almost every key now maps to a different node, so nearly all the data has to move at once [[karger]].

Consistent hashing was designed to fix exactly this. It arranges both the keys and the nodes on the same circle of hash values, and a key is owned by the first node found going around the circle. When a node joins or leaves, only the keys near it change hands; the rest stay put [[karger]].

The payoff is a precise bound: on average only about one over the number of nodes of the keys move when the node set changes, instead of nearly all of them. That is what makes it possible to grow or shrink a cluster without a storm of data movement, and it is why real distributed caches and databases use it [[dynamo]].

terms.definition: A circle of hash values on which both keys and nodes are placed.

stages.name: How it works
body: Picture the hash values as points around a circle. Each node is hashed to a point on the circle. To place a key, hash it to its own point, then walk clockwise until you meet a node; that node owns the key. Looking up a key means hashing it and finding that same next node [[karger]].

Adding a node drops a new point on the circle. It takes over only the keys that fall between it and the previous node going backwards; every other key is untouched. Removing a node hands its keys to the next node clockwise, and again nothing else moves. This locality is the whole point [[karger]].

A plain ring can be lumpy: with few nodes, the gaps between their points are uneven, so some nodes own far more of the circle, and more keys, than others. The fix is virtual nodes, giving each physical node many points on the ring. With many small arcs each, the load evens out and removing one physical node spreads its keys across many others rather than dumping them all on one neighbour [[dynamo]].

The quality of the spread depends on the hash function being well distributed. A good hash scatters both keys and node points evenly around the circle, which is what keeps each node's share close to its fair fraction [[karger]].

terms.definition: Finding a key's owner by moving around the ring from the key to the next node.

How evenly keys are spread across nodes; virtual nodes make it more even.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Consistent hashing is usually paired with replication. A key is not only stored on its owning node but also on the next few nodes clockwise, so if the owner fails the data is still reachable. The ring doubles as the way to find the backups: they are simply the following nodes [[dynamo]].

Where the ring is managed differs by system. Dynamo-style systems let every node know the ring and route requests themselves, with no central coordinator. Redis Cluster takes a related but different approach: it divides the key space into a fixed number of hash slots and assigns slots to nodes, which keeps the mapping explicit and easy to move slot by slot [[redis-cluster]].

Even with virtual nodes, load can be uneven if some keys are far hotter than others, a hot key problem the ring alone does not solve. A single wildly popular key still lands on one node. Handling that needs extra tactics such as replicating or splitting the hot key, which is a caching and sharding concern layered on top of the ring [[redis-cluster]].

terms.definition: How many nodes hold a copy of each key, found by continuing clockwise from the owner.
A fixed partition of the key space; Redis Cluster assigns slots to nodes rather than hashing to a point directly.

A single key so popular that its one owning node is overloaded even with even hashing.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The main trade-off is between even load and simplicity. More virtual nodes per machine give a smoother spread but cost more memory and bookkeeping to track all the ring points. Fixed hash slots, as in Redis Cluster, trade some of that smoothness for a mapping that is explicit and simple to reason about and migrate [[redis-cluster]].

Consistent hashing shines when the node set changes often, which is the normal state of a large cache or store: machines fail, get replaced, and are added as traffic grows. If your node set never changed, plain modulo hashing would be fine; the technique earns its complexity precisely because real clusters are always churning [[karger]].

This idea connects the map. It is how a cache cluster, the previous topic, decides which cache holds a key, and it is one of the ways a sharded database, a later topic, decides which shard holds a row. Learning it here means replication and sharding will reuse the same ring rather than introduce it fresh [[dynamo]].

misconceptions.myth: Consistent hashing spreads keys perfectly evenly.
misconceptions.truth: A plain ring can be lumpy with few nodes; evenness comes from giving each node many virtual points [[dynamo]].

misconceptions.myth: Adding a node reshuffles all the data.
misconceptions.truth: Only the keys near the new node move; on average about one over the node count, not nearly all [[karger]].

misconceptions.myth: The ring removes hot spots entirely.
misconceptions.truth: A single very popular key still lands on one node, so hot keys need extra handling [[redis-cluster]].

misconceptions.myth: Every system places keys by walking a continuous ring.
misconceptions.truth: Redis Cluster instead uses a fixed set of hash slots assigned to nodes, a related but different design [[redis-cluster]].
